extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, and practitioners researching District of Columbia (D.C.) regulations
extracted.subtask_description: A jurisdiction-specific research guide for locating, citing, and comparing current District of Columbia regulations, proposed/final rules, and related secondary materials. Focuses on which primary sources to consult and how to cite and track regulatory history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the D.C. Municipal Regulations (D.C.M.R.) for current codified regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C.M.R. is the current code of District of Columbia regulations and should be consulted for the codified, current regulatory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DCMR provides regulatory history beginning April 2009 and includes citations to the D.C. Register where the original text of a regulation is published. Use the D.C.M.R. as the primary source for finding the current, codified regulatory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bluebook citation format for D.C. Municipal Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: How to cite a D.C.M.R. provision in Bluebook format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: D.C. Mun. Regs. tit. 20, § 4305 (2005). Explanation of components: 'D.C. Mun. Regs.' = D.C. Municipal Regulations; 'tit. 20' = title number representing a topic (e.g., title 20 = environment); '43' = chapter number within title; '4305' = section number; '2005' = year of latest amended version of the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use code-compare tools (Lexis 'Compare Versions') to detect text changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When researching regulatory history or changes, compare different editions/versions to identify additions and deletions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lexis's 'Compare Versions' tool to compare editions of the D.C.M.R.; text added in a newer version and text removed from an earlier version are highlighted. The tool is also available for D.C. Code research. Do not rely solely on a single printed or online edition when tracking amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the D.C. Register (D.C. Reg.) for proposed and final regulations and agency notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Register is the official weekly publication for proposed and final agency regulations, notices, public hearings, and other documents of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office of Documents and Administrative Issuances publishes the D.C. Register every Friday (or next business day if Friday is a public holiday). The Register includes Council acts, laws, resolutions, notices of emergency/proposed/final agency regulations, notices of public hearings, and other public-interest documents. Use it to find rulemaking notices, publication dates, and related docket information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bluebook citation format for the D.C. Register
rubrics_metrics.description: How to cite an item in the D.C. Register using Bluebook conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 51 D.C. Reg. 1541 (April 16, 2004). Explanation: '51' = volume of the D.C. Register; 'D.C. Reg.' = D.C. Register; '1541' = page number in that issue; the parenthetical date is the issue date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish current sources from historical materials and consult historical-research resources when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: This guide focuses on current sources; historical D.C. regulations and their research methods are covered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need historical versions of regulations or older regulatory history prior to April 2009, consult the guide's Historical Research section and the listed historical resources (other library holdings, archives, and historical indexes). Do not assume current codified text reflects historical positions without checking historical sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of access restrictions and use appropriate subscription databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some regulatory resources are available only through subscription databases or library collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide marks resources with icons indicating access: Library Collection, Website, Subscription Database (Law School Only), Subscription Database (University-wide). Examples of subscription databases include Bloomberg Law, Lexis, and Westlaw (password required). Confirm access rights and use institution subscriptions where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult secondary guides and related research aids for locating D.C. regulatory materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use related practice manuals, law library guides, and online directories to supplement primary-source searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related resources listed include 'Chapter 1: Finding the Law' in The District of Columbia Practice Manual (District of Columbia Bar), District of Columbia Resources (Georgetown Law Library), and Guide to Law Online: U.S. Washington, D.C. (Law Library of Congress). These secondary sources can provide search strategies, context, and pointers to additional primary materials.
